items.prompt: White to move. The black king sits in the corner and the white king is a knight's move away. Find checkmate in one.

claims.statement: After Rh1 the king on b3 covers a2.

hints: Which squares next to the black king does the white king already cover?
The king on b3 covers a2 and b2. Only b1 is left for the black king.
A rook check along the first rank also takes b1 away.
items.explain: The king on b3 covers a2 and b2. The rook check along the first rank covers b1 and gives check at the same time, so the king on a1 has no square left.

feedback_by_move.h4h2: Rh2 attacks a2 and b2 but gives no check; the king has b1 and Black is not mated.
feedback_by_move.h4a4: Ra4 cuts the a-file but gives no check, so it is not mate.

items.prompt: White to move. The kings face each other with one square between them. Find the rook check that drives the black king back a rank.

claims.statement: Rh6 is legal and gives check.
After Rh6+ the black king has three squares, all on the seventh rank.

hints: Which rank is the black king on? A rook can check along a rank from far away.
The white king already covers the squares in front of the black king, so a check can only send it backwards.
Slide the rook to the sixth rank on the far side of the board.
items.explain: Rh6+ checks along the sixth rank from a square the black king can never reach. The white king covers c5, d5 and e5, so Black has only c7, d7 and e7: the king is pushed back one rank, and the tablebase confirms White still wins.

feedback_by_move.h1h5: Rh5 gives no check, so Black is free to step sideways and nothing is pushed back.

items.prompt: White to move. Find checkmate in one.
hints: The black king is in the corner. Which squares can it use?
The king on f7 and the rook on g6 cover everything except h7.
A rook check along the h-file takes h7 away and attacks the king.
items.explain: Rh6 checks along the h-file while the white king covers g7 and g8: mate. A quiet move such as Rg7 would leave Black with no move and no check, which is stalemate.

feedback_by_move.g6g7: Rg7 takes every square from the king but gives no check: stalemate, a draw.

items.prompt: White could also play Rg7, which takes away every square from the black king. Does that keep the win? Predict, then check.
hints: After Rg7, does Black have any legal move?
Is the black king in check after Rg7?
No check and no legal move is stalemate.
items.explain: After Rg7 the black king on h8 has no legal move and is not in check. That is stalemate and the game is drawn. Taking every square is not enough: the last move must also give check.

items.prompt: White to move. Find checkmate in one.
hints: Which squares next to the black king does the white king already cover?
Only h2 is free for the black king.
A check along the h-file takes h2 away.
items.explain: The white king covers g1 and g2. Rh5 gives check along the h-file and covers h2: mate. Rb2 would cover h2 along the second rank without a check, and Black would have no move: stalemate.

feedback_by_move.b5b2: Rb2 leaves Black with no legal move and no check: stalemate, a draw.

items.prompt: White to move. Find a move that keeps the win.

claims.statement: The rook on d4 is attacked and undefended.

hints: Look at what the black king attacks.
The rook is attacked and nothing protects it.
Move the rook to a square the black king cannot reach, ideally far from it.
items.explain: The black king attacks the rook on d4 and nothing protects it. A move that leaves the rook next to the king, or ignores the attack, lets Black take it, and the game is a bare-king draw.

feedback_by_move.a1b2: Kb2 ignores the attack: Black takes the rook and it is a draw.
feedback_by_move.d4b4: Rb4 lands next to the black king with no protection.
feedback_by_move.d4d6: Rd6 is also next to the black king and unprotected.
feedback_by_move.d4c4: Rc4+ is a check, but the king simply takes the rook.
feedback_by_move.d4d5: Rd5+ is a check next to the king with no protection: the king takes it.

items.prompt: Black to move. With best play, is this a win for White or a draw?

claims.statement: The rook on d4 is loose.

hints: Is anything of White's attacked?
Does anything protect the rook on d4?
What is left on the board after the rook is taken?
items.explain: The king captures the rook and the position is a bare king against a bare king, a draw. Having the move matters: if it were White's turn, the rook could still run away.

items.prompt: White to move. With best play, can White force checkmate?
hints: Count the pieces on each side.
Black has more than a bare king.
A bishop gives the defender a piece to protect with and extra squares.
items.explain: In this position the tablebase says draw. Rook against bishop is usually a draw, though some positions are won. [I] The bishop and king can protect each other, so the king is not easily fenced to the edge.

items.prompt: White to move. With best play, can White force checkmate?
hints: Count the pieces on each side.
Black has a rook too. Can a fence hold a king that has its own rook?
A defending rook can check and attack, and the king stays out of any box.
items.explain: In this position the tablebase says draw. Rook against rook is usually a draw, though some positions are won (skewers, forks). [I] Fencing works because a lone king has no piece of its own to fight back with.

items.prompt: You are White. Checkmate within 40 moves.

claims.statement: White wins by force from here.

hints: Fence the king with the rook from far away.
Bring your own king up beside it before you check.
Never leave the rook next to the black king without a guard, and look for stalemate before each quiet move.
items.explain: This is the whole method in play: a rook fence from a distance, the king up to meet the enemy king, and a check on the edge only when the king guards the checking square.

items.prompt: White could play the king move Kb2 instead, bringing the king closer. Does that keep the win? Predict, then check.
hints: What does the black king attack right now?
After Kb2, can the black king take something?
What is left on the board then?
items.explain: Bringing the king up is the right plan only when nothing is loose. Here the rook is attacked first. After Kb2 the black king takes the rook and the game is drawn.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the one move that forces checkmate in two.

claims.statement: The move forces mate on the next move.

hints: Which squares does the black king have now?
The white king can take two more of them in a single step.
Step the king so that it stands a knight's move from the corner.
items.explain: The king step to c7 covers b8 and b7, so the black king has only a7. Then a rook check along the a-file is mate, because the king on c7 also covers b6.

items.prompt: White to move. Find a move that keeps the win.

claims.statement: The rook on c8 is attacked and undefended.

hints: What has the black king just done?
The black king is next to the rook and nothing guards it.
Move the rook to any square the black king cannot reach, ideally one that keeps the c-file closed.
items.explain: The black king stepped to b7 and attacks the unprotected rook on c8. The rook must go to a square the king cannot reach. Staying on the c-file keeps the fence closed; any move next to the king, or a king move, throws the win away.

feedback_by_move.d4c4: Kc4 leaves the rook en prise: the king takes it and the game is drawn.
feedback_by_move.c8a8: Ra8 lands next to the black king and is unprotected.
feedback_by_move.c8c7: Rc7+ is check next to the king with no guard: the king takes the rook.
feedback_by_move.c8c6: Rc6 is next to the king and unprotected.

items.prompt: You are White. Checkmate within 6 moves.

claims.statement: White wins by force from here.
White mates in at most three moves.

hints: Black has one move now. Take squares away with the king.
The king and the rook must stand so that the last check cannot be answered.
The rook is guarded by the king; the last check comes along the back rank.
items.explain: This is the end of the method: the king closes in, Black has one move at a time, and the rook gives the last check along the edge when the king guards the squares in front.

items.prompt: White to move. With best play, can White force checkmate?

claims.statement: White wins by force from here.

hints: Is White's rook attacked?
Does Black have anything besides a king?
A lone king and a safe rook on the board: is that enough with the king helping?
items.explain: Nothing of White's is loose and Black has only a king, so the method works: fence, bring the king, check on the edge.
